title: A Simple Way To Get Better At Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin proposes a low-effort daily habit for improving classroom management: keeping a written record of every misbehavior, the specific behavior, and the consequence given, reviewed briefly at the end of each day. He grounds the idea in research on self-monitoring, citing a large Kaiser Permanente weight-loss trial in which food-journal keepers lost roughly twice as much weight as non-journalers, and comparing the effect to video-game scoring systems that motivate improvement simply through visible tracking. He argues the mechanism is psychological rather than strategic — the act of noticing and recording naturally increases consistency and reliance on one's classroom management plan, independent of any specific new technique. Beyond behavior counts dropping over time, he frames the exercise as reorienting a teacher's focus away from frustration with students and toward their own agency and performance, which he presents as the deeper lesson of the practice.
points: Keeping a brief written daily record of every misbehavior and its consequence is proposed as a simple habit that improves consistency over time.
The recommendation is grounded in self-monitoring research, including a cited Kaiser Permanente trial where food-journal keepers lost roughly twice as much weight as non-journalers.
Tracking works psychologically, similar to video-game scoring systems, by creating an internal motivation to improve simply through visible numbers.
The specific record should include the rule broken, the exact behavior, the consequence given, and a daily total reviewed at day's end and again the next morning.
The practice reorients a teacher's focus away from frustration with students and toward their own performance and agency.
quotes: It’s to keep a record of every misbehavior. You see, the simple act of tracking is shown to improve performance no matter the field.

According to research, keeping a journal of everything you eat results in greater weight loss. (One 1,700 person clinical trial at Kaiser Permanente showed twice as much weight loss as those who didn’t keep a journal.)
Keeping score, so to speak, sparks an intense desire to improve—even if you do nothing else but notice your numbers, regardless of whether they went up or down.
Practically, what keeping a record does for classroom management is cause you to be more consistent.
It also helps shift your focus away from your students, and how their misbehavior annoys and frustrates you, and toward your ability to influence and change their behavior.
It shows you in a way you can’t deny that it’s not about your students. It’s about you and your own performance.
